extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of classical mechanics (readers of Newton's Principia), mathematicians and physicists interested in theoretical mechanics and hydrostatics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracted section of Newton's Principia (Latin) presenting examples, rules, lemmas and propositions about motion in resisting media, spirals, and hydrostatics. Contains worked examples, regulæ, theorems with corollaries and problems showing how to derive densities, forces, times and spaces under various resistance laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exempl. 4: Hyperbola AGK and medium density law
rubrics_metrics.description: Given AGK a hyperbola with center X and asymptotes MX, NX defined so that, with rectangle XZDN constructed meeting the hyperbola in G and its asymptote in V, VG is reciprocally as some power ND^n; find the medium density making a projectile move on that hyperbola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets DN, BD, NX to A, O, C and expresses VG = bb ÷ (A - O)^n; expands bb ÷ (A - O)^n into an infinite series and identifies series terms to substitute into Qo, Ro^2, So^3, yielding a formula for medium density S ÷ (R × sqrt(1 + QQ)) at a point G with an explicit algebraic expression. Concludes resistances and velocities at G correspond to given ratios and gives procedures to compute curve and related quantities; leads into subsequent Regulæ (1–8).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium on Hyperbolas vs Parabolas
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that motion in a parabola occurs only in nonresisting media, while the hyperbolas described here occur under perpetual resistance; the uniformly resisting-medium trajectory approaches these hyperbolas closer than a parabola.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that the described hyperbolic curves are of hyperbolic kind but differ near the vertex from the hyperbolas constructed earlier; they are useful in practice and sometimes preferable. Connects construction of tangents and relations of density, velocity and resistance (density reciprocal to tangent GT, velocity proportional to sqrt(GT^2 ÷ GV), resistance to gravity as GT to (3n^2+3n)/(n+2) × GV). Leads to explicit Rules (Reg. 1–8) for practical determination and correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reg. 1
rubrics_metrics.description: If medium density at A is held fixed and angle NAH is varied, the lengths AH, AI, HX remain fixed; thus if those lengths can be found in any case, the hyperbola is readily determined from any given angle NAH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rule for constructing the curve given density at A and an angle: AH, AI, HX are invariants when density fixed and angle varied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reg. 2
rubrics_metrics.description: If both the angle NAH and the medium density at A are held fixed and the projectile's launch velocity changes, AH remains fixed while AI changes in the duplicate reciprocal ratio of the velocity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives how AI scales with changes of launch speed when angle and local density are fixed: AI varies inversely as velocity squared (duplicate reciprocal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reg. 3
rubrics_metrics.description: If angle NAH, projectile velocity at A, and the accelerating gravity are all fixed, and the proportion of resistance at A to the moving gravity is increased by any factor, the ratio AH to AI is increased by the same factor while the parabola's latus rectum (and AH^2 ÷ AI) scales proportionally; therefore AH and AI are decreased accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains how changes in the proportion resistance:weight (e.g., via specific gravity or medium density) affect AH and AI; notes that resistance may diminish less rapidly with size than weight, altering proportions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reg. 4
rubrics_metrics.description: Because medium density near the hyperbola's vertex is larger than at A, to keep a mean density one must find the ratio of the smallest tangent GT to the tangent at AH and decrease the density at A according to Rule 3 by a little less than the semi-sum of those tangents to the tangent at AH.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives a correction to assumed density at A to account for variation of density near the vertex; a practical correction when using mean density.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reg. 5
rubrics_metrics.description: Given AH, AI, and wanting to describe AGK: extend HN to X so HX equals (n+1)-th power of AI; with center X and asymptotes MX, NX describe Hyperbola through A so that AI to any VG equals XV^n to XI^n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit constructive rule for producing the hyperbola from given lengths AH, AI by relating AI and VG via powers and asymptotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reg. 6
rubrics_metrics.description: The larger the exponent n, the more accurate these hyperbolas become for the ascending part of the projectile from A, and the less accurate for the descent; conversely for smaller n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses relative accuracy of these hyperbolas versus conic parabolas and practical choice of n; provides method to find impact point K on a line through A by intersecting asymptotes and taking NK equal to AM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reg. 7
rubrics_metrics.description: Method for determining the hyperbola from phenomena: fire two equal projectiles with same speed at different angles, note impact points K and k and the proportion AK:Ak = d:e; use graphical construction with assumed AH to find AK,Ak and iterate (using Reg. 6) to find AH such that AK:Ak matches d:e.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A practical experimental / graphical method for deducing AH (and thus the hyperbola) from measured ranges at two angles: erect perpendicular, assume AH, draw AK,Ak, compare ratios and adjust using a constructed line SM and perpendicular MN for the differential; iterate with several assumptions to obtain regular curve NNXN and locate AH by intersection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reg. 8
rubrics_metrics.description: Given AH and HX and wanting the position of line AH such that a projectile launched from A with given velocity strikes any given point K: erect perpendiculars AC and KF at A and K to the horizon with AC downward equal to AI (½HX); through AK and KF describe a hyperbola whose conjugate passes through C, with center A and circle of radius AH cutting the hyperbola at H; then the projectile along AH will hit K.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive geometric method: use equalities AE = AM and KN = AE to argue that CE = FH so H lies on the hyperbola and circle intersection; applies whether AKN is parallel to horizon or inclined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XI (Theor. VIII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body is resisted partly in ratio to velocity and partly in ratio to square of velocity, and moved only by an innate force in a similar medium, and if times are taken in arithmetic progression, then the quantities reciprocally proportional to the velocities (with a given added quantity) will be in geometric progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by constructing a rectangular-hyperbola figure with area representing time increasing uniformly; shows that 1/GD decreases like the velocity under the given resistance law which is the sum of terms proportional to velocity and velocity^2; leads to the conclusion that 1/GD (reciprocal of GD) is proportional to velocity and that sums CG+GD grow geometrically with uniform area increments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. XI
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol. 1: If times are proportional to hyperbolic areas ABED, velocity can be represented by the reciprocal 1/GD. Corol. 2: Given initial and final reciprocal velocities, one can find point G; then velocities at other times follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives practical method to map time to velocity and vice versa via the geometric construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XII (Theor. IX)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the same hypotheses, if spaces described are taken in arithmetic progression, then velocities (augmented by a given amount) will be in geometric progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses an asymptote construction and hyperbolic area RSED representing space; shows that decrements of GD relate to fixed increments of space leading to velocities represented by length GD forming a geometric progression while space increases arithmetically. Corollaries provide constructions to find G from given velocities and spaces and vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIII (Theor. X)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a body attracted by uniform gravity along a straight line and resisted partly in ratio to velocity and partly to velocity^2: then when straight lines parallel to diameters of certain circles and hyperbolae are drawn, velocities are proportional to certain segments dropped from a given point and times are proportional to sectors (areas) of those circles or hyperbolae; and conversely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treats three cases (ascending with circle quadrants, ascending with hyperbola construction, descending) showing area-as-time correspondences: velocities ~ certain segments (AP), times ~ sectors (EDT or hyperbolic sectors). Provides a corollary comparing velocities in resisting vs nonresisting media by comparing triangle areas and sector areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIV (Prob. IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: With forces composed of resistance and gravity in geometric progression, the space of ascent or descent is the sum or difference of the area through which time is represented and the area of another figure which increases or decreases in arithmetic progression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructs lines proportional to gravity and resistance and shows how areas corresponding to time and additional constructed areas give the distance from maximum altitude as the excess of one area over another; provides formulae and a corollary linking space described in resisting vs non-resisting media via proportional areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma III (on a spiral and tangents)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a spiral PQR which meets all radii SP, SQ, SR at equal angles, with PT tangent at P meeting SQ at T and PO, QO perpendiculars to the spiral meeting in O and SO joined: as P and Q coalesce, angle PSO tends to a right angle, and the ultimate ratio of rectangle TQ × PS to PQ^2 is a ratio of equality (i.e., TQ × PS = PQ^2 in the limit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides geometric relationships involving perpendiculars to the spiral and limits used later in spiral motion proofs; deduces PQ^2 = TQ × PS in the limiting/coincident case which is used to relate generated impulses to arc lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XV (Theor. XI)
rubrics_metrics.description: If medium density at each place is reciprocal to the distance of the place from a fixed center, and the centripetal force is in the duplicate ratio of the density, then a body can revolve in a spiral that cuts every radius from that center at a given angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developed from Lemma III: by considering equal time arcs and areas and neglecting resistance compared to centripetal force, shows velocities scale as 1/sqrt(SP) and deduces the form of resistance and density. Corollaries: velocity at P equals that for circular motion at same radius; expressions for density as OS/OP or OS/(OP×SP); relations between resistance and centripetal force (½OS:OP); conditions for possible gyration (resistance must be less than half centripetal force), and consequences for revolution counts and times relative to circle perimeters and densities. Includes methods to adapt spirals to different densities and to deduce motion properties in other regular density laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVI (Theor. XII)
rubrics_metrics.description: If medium density at places is reciprocal to some power of the distance from a center (density ∝ 1/SP^n), and the centripetal force is reciprocal to distance raised to that power (force ∝ 1/SP^{n+1}), then a body can move in a spiral cutting all radii at a given angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generalizes Prop. XV: time to describe arc PQ ∝ PQ × SP^{n/2}; resistance in P ∝ Rr/(PQ^2 × SP^n) leading to density in P ∝ 1/SP^n. Scholium notes these propositions assume motions small enough to ignore density variation across the body's dimensions and that density should be adjusted where resistance law does not follow density exactly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVII (Prob. V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: Given a spiral and desired law, find the centripetal force and medium resistance that will make a body revolve in that given spiral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: from the velocity (from given centripetal force) and the altitude TQ (proportional to centripetal force × time^2) obtain the generated force; from differences of equal-area time-elements obtain retardation and hence resistance and medium density, following the method used in Prop. XV.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XVIII (Prob. VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem: Given the law of centripetal force, find the medium density at each place that will make a body describe a given spiral.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outline: compute velocities from the centripetal force law; deduce retardations from velocity decrements and thus infer medium density as in previous propositions (XV–XVII). The text notes the general method was opened earlier and the author will not prolong the discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: Fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluidum est corpus omne cujus partes cedunt vi cuicunque illatæ, & cedendo facile movetur inter se.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defines a fluid as any body whose parts yield to any impressed force and readily move among themselves; sets stage for hydrostatic propositions that follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XIX (Theor. XIII) on pressure in closed homogeneous immobile fluids
rubrics_metrics.description: In a homogeneous immobile fluid confined in any vessel and compressed everywhere (setting aside condensation, gravity and all centripetal forces), all parts are pressed equally in every direction and remain at rest under that pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrated by considering spherical partitions and arguing that unequal pressure would lead to motion and contradiction; includes seven cases showing immobility and equal pressure on all spherical parts, consequences for a nonrigid vessel, and a corollary that parts of a fluid are not set into motion by pressure applied externally except insofar as surface shape changes or the parts change their relative pressing. This proposition underpins later hydrostatic results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XX (Theor. XIV) on pressure on the bottom of a spherical fluid
rubrics_metrics.description: For spherical fluid shells homogeneous and at equal distances from the center, each part inclining toward the center, the bottom (fundum) sustains the weight of a cylinder whose base equals the bottom's area and whose height equals the fluid depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Divides fluid into concentric thin spherical layers and argues that the pressure on the bottom equals the gravity of an equivalent solid cylinder (limit as layers become infinitesimally thin). Corollaries: the bottom is not urged by the whole fluid weight but only by the described part; equal pressures occur for surfaces at equal distances regardless of orientation or internal flow; heavy parts of fluid do not gain motion from the pressure of overlying fluid absent condensation.
